_comment: The per-service baseline for PROVIDER deployments — the other half of the code root.
brokerimages.json pins the guest OS a provider boots (trust-chain hop 3); it says
nothing about the containers inside, because mr_config_id commits to the app-compose
the OPERATOR chose. This file records which containers we have reviewed.
ONE FILE, SEVERAL DEPLOYMENTS. A fleet runs several deployments — the 2026-10-10 sweep
found five among seven providers — so the file records several, each keyed by the
CONTRACT its providers are registered on and the PROVIDER ADDRESSES that run it. Not by
compose_hash: that moves on any edit to the app-compose, including ones that change
nothing about what runs (cn-1 and cn-4 differ only in the app-compose `name`, and their
service blocks are byte-identical). The contract is in the key because one operator
key may be registered on testnet and mainnet and run a different deployment on each.
A PROVIDER WITH NO DEPLOYMENT HERE IS NOT COMPARED, and `pcverify -provider` says so
and exits 3 — the same 'did not run' an empty file gives. It is never compared against
some other provider's deployment: that would list every difference between two
deployments and say nothing except that nobody recorded this one. Not recorded is
unverified, not refuted.
WHAT IS RECORDED, AND WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT.
`mainnet compute-network-20` — recorded 2026-08-28 from that provider's own
`pcverify -blocks` output and re-confirmed against a live run on 2026-10-10.
`testnet compute-network-20-dev` — recorded 2026-10-15, broker v0.5.4, checked against
the live provider with `pcverify -strict -app-baseline`: 11 of 11, exit 0, and a
one-character edit to the recorded model revision made that run fail on that line.
The other mainnet providers are NOT recorded. They run broker builds that
the release provenance policy does not accept (v0.5.2, and two manual branch builds
from docker-publish.yml), and the broker team's v0.5.4 rollout will change their manifests anyway.
Recording them now would freeze controllers that predate the fixes v0.5.4 carries.
RECORDING IS NOT APPROVAL, and the mainnet entry is the case in point. Its three
broker-image services run v0.5.1, a real release below the policy's v0.5.4 floor, so
they MISMATCH under the release rule until that provider moves to v0.5.4 — and the
review still reports ten blocking findings on it. It stays recorded because the
other nine services are worth holding still: from here a change to any of them is a
mismatch named with the first differing line, not something nobody notices.
WHAT THIS FILE CANNOT SEE. compose_hash describes what BOOTED. On v0.5.4 the
controller may swap the broker and event images and change the upstream set at
runtime; those changes leave compose_hash alone and are recorded only in RTMR3. A
match here says the deployment booted as recorded, not that it is still running as
recorded. Reading RTMR3 is a separate check (client/evidence/rtmr3.go), which pcverify
runs beside this one.
HOW A DEPLOYMENT IS WRITTEN. Run `pcverify -provider <addr> -blocks` (with
-chain-rpc-url and -serving-contract for a non-default chain). It prints, per
service, the canonical block and — labelled `no-image:` — the same block with the
image identity held out, and then each top-level section (`top-level volumes`, …).
Copy the one each service's rule needs into `block`, one
array element per line, mechanically rather than by hand. Then check the candidate
against the live provider with `-strict -app-baseline <file>` before committing it.
Text rather than a digest, deliberately: both sides are loaded with docker compose's
own loader (compose-go v2.0.2, composeload.go) and reduced by the same renderer at
comparison time, so library formatting cancels out, and a broker upgrade arrives as a
legible diff. The canonical form is a COMPARISON form — keys sorted, short syntax
rewritten long as the loader does, quoting normalized, YAML anchors expanded, and a
held-out image reads `<image-held-out>` — not deployable YAML. The blocks below were
regenerated in that form on 2026-10-16; every one of them reduces to exactly what the
earlier, hand-ordered text did.
THERE IS ONE IMAGE RULE. `image` omitted (the default) means the recorded block
contains the image line and pins the reference exactly as written. `"image":
{"repository": "ghcr.io/..."}` means any RELEASED build of that repository — a
digest whose signed release provenance pcverify and the sealing path verify at run time (client/provenance) — and records the `no-image:` block instead. It
exists for 0G's own broker image, which moves on every broker release; it is used
nowhere else. There is deliberately no `digest` or `reference` rule: the block already
says the reference, and a second statement of it could only disagree.
WHAT A MATCH REQUIRES (evidence.CheckCompose): every service the deployment records
present exactly once, every service in the manifest recorded, each block equal after
reduction, and each image satisfying its rule. A service the deployment does not
record is a MISMATCH — an unlisted container is unreviewed code in the same guest.
The same holds for the top-level sections other than services and `x-` extensions
(`top_level`): each recorded one present and equal, and none unrecorded. They are
what a service's volumes and networks resolve to — a declaration changed to an nfs
driver moves the data behind a name while every service block still matches. A
deployment with no `top_level` allows none.
AN EMPTY `deployments` LIST means NOT CONFIGURED: nothing is compared, warn mode
proceeds and says so, enforce refuses every provider and names the configuration. It
never means 'accept anything'.
Fields. Deployment: `name` (unique), `contract`, `providers` (addresses; any case),
`note`, `services`, `top_level`. Service: `name` (the compose key), `image` (the rule above),
`block` (canonical text, one element per line), `note`. Notes are the audit record and
are never read by the comparison. Top-level section: `key`, `block`, `note`.

deployments.name: mainnet compute-network-20
note: mainnet compute-network-20, model 0GM-1.0-35B-A3B, guest OS dstack-nvidia-0.5.9,
Broker image v0.5.1 (sha256:ec5df834…) — a tagged release, not a listed one.

services.name: broker-ingress
note: dstack's own TLS terminator, pinned by digest. Holds /var/run/dstack.sock, which
the review reports to justify: a container with the guest-agent socket can derive
the app's keys and obtain quotes in the app's name. Accepted here because that is
precisely this service's job — the cert-binding quote the gateway verifies in
`pcverify -gateway` is the one this container obtains. The socket is why it must be
recorded, not why it should be removed.
block: - DOMAIN=${DOMAIN:?set DOMAIN — there is no default, so that a missing value cannot point this deployment at production}

services.name: 0gm-sglang
note: The model server, pinned by digest. Recording the block freezes --model-path and
--revision, which is the most load-bearing text in this entry: an unfrozen revision
means the weights answering a sealed prompt are the operator's later choice.
`ipc: host` is a review justify — shared memory is a channel nothing else in the
manifest names — and is accepted because the CVM is one guest and this is the
process the shared memory belongs to.

services.name: mysql
note: Pinned by digest. The root and user credentials are literals in the manifest, which
the review has no rule for and which is worth saying anyway: it is acceptable only
because the database is reachable on the compose network alone, never from outside
the guest. If a future manifest publishes a port for it, this note stops holding.

services.name: broker-config-init
note: Pinned by digest, and the reason to record it is the `command` text rather than the
image: this is the script that materializes config.yaml from BROKER_CONFIG and
substitutes PRIVATE_KEY into it. No image digest covers that script — only this
block does — so it is TCB the compose hash alone pins, and freezing it here is what
makes a change to how the broker's key is placed into the guest visible.
block: # First boot only. The controller's PUT /v1/config/core writes this same
# file and records the change in RTMR3, so rewriting it on every start
# would silently undo an operator change that is already on-chain — the
# same guard dstack's own boot script puts on docker-compose.yaml.
echo "BROKER_CONFIG is empty and no config exists yet" >&2
# Rename last, so a container killed mid-write leaves no half-file that
# the guard above would then accept as complete.

services.name: 0g-serving-provider-broker
note: 0G's own broker image, under the release rule. cn-20 runs v0.5.1, which
the release provenance policy refuses (below its v0.5.4 floor), so this service mismatches on its image until the
provider moves to an accepted release; the block itself matches. The digest also appears
in IMAGE_DIGEST, which is why the hold-out erases the image IDENTITY wherever it
appears rather than just deleting the `image` key.
Two relative bind mounts (./logs/broker, ./logs/event) are review justifies: what a
relative bind exposes depends on the directory the deployment was brought up from.

services.name: 0g-serving-provider-event
note: Same image and release rule as the broker service, and the same v0.5.1 mismatch.
Mounts ./logs/event, a relative bind the review justifies.

services.name: 0g-controller
note: Same image and release rule, and the same v0.5.1 mismatch. Mounts BOTH host sockets:
/var/run/dstack.sock (review justify) and /var/run/docker.sock (review BLOCKING).
The broker team's answer to why the controller holds docker.sock is #759 — it swaps
broker/event images, may create no new container without ZG_CONTROLLER_ENGINES=on,
and records each swap in RTMR3 first — but that is controller CODE from v0.5.4 on.
On v0.5.1 those constraints do not hold, which is why the review keeps this finding
blocking here rather than relaxing it as it does for a verified release.
Also mounts ./logs/controller, a relative bind the review justifies.

services.name: prometheus-init
note: Pinned by digest. Like broker-config-init, recorded for its `command` rather than
its image — the default scrape config is generated here, and freezing it fixes what
the monitoring stack is pointed at.

services.name: prometheus
note: Review BLOCKING: prom/prometheus:v2.45.2 is pinned by tag, not digest. Recorded as
the deployment has it, which means this entry pins a NAME — the registry can
republish that tag after the measurement and the compose hash will not move. The
block still pins everything else, so the mount set and scrape target cannot change
silently, but the code behind the name can. This must become digest-pinned.

services.name: grafana
note: Review BLOCKING: grafana/grafana-oss:11.4.0 is pinned by tag — same consequence as
the prometheus entry above, and the same required change. Also two relative bind
mounts (./grafana/provisioning, ./grafana/dashboards): unlike the log binds
elsewhere, these are READ by the container, so what dashboards and datasources it
loads comes from a host directory the manifest does not describe.

services.name: prometheus-node-exporter
note: The worst entry in this file, and recorded anyway so it cannot get worse unnoticed.
FIVE review blockings: the image is pinned by tag; `privileged: true`; and `/`,
`/proc` and `/sys` each mounted from the host. Privileged inside a CVM means the
container holds every capability and sees every host device the guest has, which makes
the whole guest one trust domain — so no per-service reasoning in this file holds
beneath it, and recording the block does not repair that. What recording buys is that
the mount set and the command are frozen. Host metrics do not require this much: a
node exporter reading /proc and /sys read-only does not need `privileged` or `/`.

services.name: dcgm-exporter
note: Two review blockings: the image is pinned by tag, and cap_add grants SYS_ADMIN.
SYS_ADMIN is close to root on the guest and is the capability most container escapes
reach for. GPU profiling metrics are the usual reason an exporter is given it, which
is a reason and not a justification — the metrics are monitoring, and the capability
is inside the boundary that holds sealed prompts.
Every named volume the services mount, each a bare declaration: an ordinary local
volume the CVM creates on its own disk. Recorded because a service block only names
a volume; a declaration changed to an nfs/cifs driver, a bind of another path, or
external: true would move the data behind that name — the ingress TLS key, the
database, the broker config — while every service block still matched.
The one project network, created by this manifest (external: false).

deployments.name: testnet compute-network-20-dev
note: testnet compute-network-20-dev, model 0GM-1.0-35B-A3B, guest OS dstack-nvidia-0.5.9,
compose_hash 9b0de348d56a36391d4474913efd75dcdaf109e4c11ccb79d5cd08f424bcade3, broker
v0.5.4 (sha256:951f4c79…). The deployment the broker team normalized for the v0.5.4
rollout. The review reports no blocking finding on it: its one candidate,
0g-controller's docker.sock, meets every condition of the controller exception and is
reported at justify. cn-20 has ten.

services.name: broker-ingress
note: dstack's TLS terminator. No longer mounts /var/run/dstack.sock (broker #763): it
mounts the zg-tee-ro volume and its entrypoint symlinks the read-only attestation
proxy socket to /var/run/dstack.sock, so the ingress code is unchanged while the only
calls that reach the guest agent are /Info and /GetQuote. The proxy is served by
0g-controller; a container on zg-tee-ro cannot reach /Sign or EmitEvent.
block: - DOMAIN=${TESTNET_DOMAIN:?set TESTNET_DOMAIN — there is no default, so that a missing value cannot point this deployment at production}

services.name: 0gm-sglang
note: The model server. Recording the block freezes --model-path and --revision, which is
the most load-bearing text in it. `ipc: host` is a review justify, accepted because
the shared memory belongs to this process inside one guest.

services.name: mysql
note: Credentials are literals in the manifest (MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=123456). Acceptable only
because the service publishes no port and is reachable on the compose network alone.

services.name: broker-config-init
note: Recorded for its `command`: the script that materializes the broker config and places
the private key into it. No image digest covers that script; only this block does.
block: # First boot only. The controller's PUT /v1/config/core writes this same
# file and records the change in RTMR3, so rewriting it on every start
# would silently undo an operator change that is already on-chain — the
# same guard dstack's own boot script puts on docker-compose.yaml.
echo "BROKER_CONFIG is empty and no config exists yet" >&2
# Rename last, so a container killed mid-write leaves no half-file that
# the guard above would then accept as complete.

services.name: 0g-serving-provider-broker
note: 0G's broker image, recorded by repository so a release does not force a gateway
release. The block still carries TARGET_URL=http://0gm-sglang:8000/v1, so it is
specific to this provider's upstream: a provider whose upstream has another service
name has a different broker block, and cannot share this one as a template.

services.name: 0g-serving-provider-event
note: Same image and the same repository rule as the broker service.

services.name: 0g-controller
note: Same image and repository rule. Holds BOTH host sockets: /var/run/dstack.sock (the
only service that does, after #763 — it serves the zg-tee and read-only zg-tee-ro
proxies) and /var/run/docker.sock. The review reports the second at JUSTIFY, not
blocking: this is a verified release, run as the 0g-controller program, with only the
keys, environment variables and healthcheck the exception covers, nothing interpolated in its service,
no host path beyond the two sockets (its logs are on a declared named volume), and
ZG_CONTROLLER_ENGINES absent — the conditions under which broker
#759 limits what it does with the socket (evidence/compose/composecontroller.go). Those limits
are the controller's code at this digest, which is why the release has to be verified.

services.name: prometheus-init
note: Recorded for its `command`: it generates the default scrape configuration.

services.name: prometheus
note: Pinned by digest.

services.name: grafana
note: Pinned by digest. Two relative bind mounts (./grafana/provisioning, ./grafana/dashboards)
are READ by the container, so the dashboards and datasources it loads come from a host
directory the manifest does not describe.

services.name: dcgm-exporter
note: Pinned by digest, and no cap_add: the SYS_ADMIN grant the mainnet deployments carry is
gone in this one.
Every named volume the services mount, each a bare declaration: an ordinary local
volume the CVM creates on its own disk. Recorded because a service block only names
a volume; a declaration changed to an nfs/cifs driver, a bind of another path, or
external: true would move the data behind that name — the ingress TLS key, the
database, the broker config — while every service block still matched.
The one project network, created by this manifest (external: false).
